---
title: "On Teaching Mathematics"
subtitle: "Goals, philosophy, and practice"
date: "2026-11-04"
---

One of my cohort members at UConn posed the following question 
as we were discussing our teaching statements:

> What is the fundamental goal of teaching mathematics?

Seemed like a pretty simple question when I first heard it ... but no
response that I could come up with on the spot felt sufficient. 
Over time my thoughts on what the overarching goal(s) are (hopefully)
be collected here, along with practices aimed at reaching them. Some entries will be from my
own stream of consciousness, others will stem from student feedback,
and others will follow from discussions with other math educators.

## I. Goals of Teaching Mathematics

### 1. Give students the tools to be independent analytical thinkers and the means to use them.

I cannot claim this as my own idea, it came from the same cohort member mentioned above (email me if you
need to cite them or something). The thought is this: what will they *really* need
in the real world? 

In the age of AI it is especially true that
computation and rote memorization are less worthwhile than ever
before; ChatGPT's most basic model can correctly answer the majority
of undergrad homework assignments and recite definitions or theorems
better than I ever could ... so what's the point? There are two answers
that come to mind.

- **Knowing what to ask.** Coming up with the right
question phrased in the right way requires fundamental understanding 
beyond memorization. 

- **Heuristic understanding, following logical arguments.** To have an intuitive understanding of
what a correct answer looks like and how to get there -- or, the ability to
*validate* answers when presented with them -- requires mathematical maturity and familiarity.



## II. Thoughts on How to Arrive at Teaching Goals

### 1. Emphasize that solving a problem should feel like defending a case in court, winning an argument, or telling a story in logic.

Many students have been shown that math is about pushing numbers and symbols around
on the page like stones in [curling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curling#Curling_stone). Up to 
a certain point this works, but it's not a robust methodology. Even though
math machinery can be [abstract nonsense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_nonsense), 
it doesn't mean we can't use words to explain ourselves! On the contrary,
**using words to justify nontrivial steps highilights the logical foundation
for the readers (and writer) of the solution/proof.**

### 2. Be Willing to Zoom Out

The meaning behind this phrase is twofold for me.

<details>
<summary><strong>See the mathematical forest through the trees.</strong></summary>
This is what
conceptual understanding is all about. We're trying to create a 
mental map that guides our arguments; to build such a thing we
have to make note of every branch and boulder, and we do this through
many examples. It would be untenable to sift through this exhaustive logbook (pun
intended) all the time, so a huge part of learning is
figuring out what the important landmarks are. 
</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Let students know you relate to them on a human level!</strong></summary>
 This gets an exclamation because it's 
often forgotten when we're laser focused on the concepts we want to help them understand; life outside
of mathematics can get lost when we dive down the rabbit hole. This can be effective with some audiences, 
wading with them into the depths of this fantasy world for an entire lecture (particularly majors or those who are acclimated
to being absorbed in abstraction), but many people appreciate coming up for air now and then. Tell a story or
a joke, make a song reference (my personal favorite), just something to let people
know that they can relax. Of course, don't waste a bunch of time
doing this or break the rhythm of your explanation, and be authentic. An
environment which lets students feel calm is more conducive to learning.
</details>

### 3. Don't Undervalue Bookkeeping

Organization plays a role in problem solving that 
often goes unnoticed. This is true in terms of identifying
hypotheses and using efficient data structures
throughout an argument, but also writing in a physically
organized fashion. As instructors we harp on readable answers because mathematics
is about the communication of ideas (rightfully so), but writing clearly
can also help the student find their way to a correct proof or numeric answer.
